old_title: Iran live: Trump says Hormuz 'sort of open' and predicts Tehran will seek peace soon
new_title: Iran live: Furious Trump condemns 'leakers' amid reports US low on precision missiles
old_text:
Donald Trump has claimed the Strait of Hormuz is "sort of open" and predicted that the war with Iran will "end pretty soon".
The US president said although the shipping route was under US control, there was a possibility that Tehran could still "shoot things" or "drop a mine."
"I think it's going to end pretty soon. I don't think they (Iran) can go much longer," Trump said in the Oval Office.
Trump also denied the US was running low on key munitions amid its war with Iran, insisting the country has "massive amounts" of ammunition and threatened lengthy prison sentences for officials who leak information about US weapons stockpiles.
The president was responding to US media reports that he had reprimanded defence secretary Pete Hegseth during a Cabinet meeting in which low ammunition stockpiles were discussed.
Earlier, Iran claimed a deal with Oman to fully open up shipping through the strait was on the brink of being agreed, with negotiations now in their "final stages". The proposed deal would give Tehran control over ships entering the Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the biggest concessions yet to Iran.
Trump makes his feelings clear about Pete Hegseth after 'treasonous leakers' rant over weapons stockpile
President Donald Trump felt the need to defend his embattled Pentagon boss, former Fox News weekend host Pete Hegseth, after a series of bombshell reports indicating that the Department of Defense has blown through nearly all the precision-guided rockets in its inventory and could take years to replenish those stocks.
In a 148-word post on Truth Social Thursday, Trump accused news organizations of "spreading false and completely unfounded rumors" about his relationship with the defense secretary and insisted he's "very happy" with Hegseth's job performance.
"Everything has been extraordinary, including our attack on Venezuela, where the result was accomplished in less than one day, allowing us to bring one of the worst criminals anywhere in the World, Nicolas Maduro, to Justice! Likewise, Iran, where the country has been decimated for the purpose of NOT ALLOWING IT TO EVER HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON, is going very well," Trump wrote.
Fallout from war in Iran is leaving millions vulnerable to hunger
As the US, Iran and Oman edge towards an interim agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, months of insecurity and disruption are leaving millions more vulnerable to hunger in Yemen.
The economic fallout from the regional conflict has driven up food and fuel prices, while more than four months of conflict with Iran has driven renewed escalation in Yemen, compounding one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
More than half the population were already facing hunger, but slow progress from world leaders to re-open the Strait has caused months of disruption to global food and energy supplies, disrupting humanitarian aid operations.
Amnesty says Gaza mass funeral highlights 'chilling' destruction of entire families
Amnesty International says a mass funeral for 112 members of the al-Hasayna and Abu Sharia families in Gaza City underscores a pattern of Israeli attacks that have wiped out entire multi-generational families.
Writing on X, Erika Guevara Rosas, Amnesty International's senior director for research, advocacy, policy and campaigns, said the victims' remains were recovered months after an Israeli strike on 23 November 2023 that reportedly killed more than 300 Palestinians.
She said recovery efforts had been delayed by Israeli restrictions on the entry of heavy equipment needed to clear rubble, with thousands of bodies still believed to be trapped beneath collapsed buildings.
"Israel must urgently allow access to Gaza for UN bodies and independent human rights investigators to preserve evidence, in line with the ICJ's orders," she added, using the acronym for the International Court of Justice.
Trump's Iran deal: Three scenarios for what could happen next
As Iran and Oman close in on a deal to open the Strait of Hormuz, there is growing optimism that the main hurdle preventing peace talks to end Donald Trump's war may be cleared.
Esmaeil Baghaei, the spokesperson for Iran's foreign ministry, said an agreement is in its "final stages", while US president Donald Trump said an "all-day negotiation" had taken place with Tehran on Tuesday.
Senior Trump administration officials, including secretary of state Marco Rubio and treasury secretary Scott Bessent, suggested a deal was imminent earlier this week - but an agreement had not been reached by Friday morning.
Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani leaders to meet in Jeddah amid Red Sea tensions
The leaders of Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are set to hold talks in Jeddah on Friday as tensions continue to rise across the Gulf and Red Sea.
It comes following Pakistan's recent decision to join a Saudi-led naval coalition aimed at countering Houthi attacks.
Pakistan's prime minister Shehbaz Sharif has arrived in the Saudi city for meetings with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdogan. The visit marks Sharif's third trip to Saudi Arabia this year.
Iran authorities announce controlled explosions in southern province
Iranian authorities announced planned controlled explosions in the southern province of Bushehr on Friday, saying blasts could be heard near the city of Khormoj between Friday morning and noon.
Officials in Dashti county did not provide further details about the purpose of the controlled explosions.
Saudi Arabia expects imminent attacks from north and south, senior official says
Saudi Arabia expects imminent coordinated attacks from the north and south by Iraqi militias and Yemen's Houthis under the supervision of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a senior Saudi official said on Thursday.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said intelligence reports from Saudi Arabia, the United States and other regional countries indicated civilian and economic sites could be targeted, including energy infrastructure, ports and airports.
Saudi Arabia had also observed drones and missiles being moved, suggesting coordinated operations from both directions, the official said.
The official said the reported threats were particularly alarming as Riyadh continued to pursue de-escalation and a negotiated settlement, adding that contacts with all parties, including Iran, and mediation efforts appeared to be moving "in the right direction." The official said the planned attacks could be intended to disrupt those diplomatic efforts.
The official said Saudi-US cooperation remained "very high" at all levels, including operationally with US Central Command, and said Saudi Arabia was prepared to take all necessary measures to respond to any aggression.
Trump says Americans will see gas for $1.85 a gallon soon. The national average is currently above $4
Donald Trump has said Americans will see gas for $1.85 a gallon soon.
"We'll see those days pretty soon again, based on everything I see", the US president told reporters Thursday. "As soon as the war ends, and I think it's going to end pretty soon".
The national average price for a gallon of gas is currently above $4. It was below $3 at the start of the Iran war in late February.
Trump denies shortage of key munitions in war with Iran
Donald Trump has denied reports that the United States is running low on key munitions amid its war with Iran, insisting the country has "massive amounts" of ammunition and threatening lengthy prison sentences for officials who leak information about US weapons stockpiles.
In a post on Truth Social on Thursday, Trump said: "Defence companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country's history."
The president claimed more weapons were being manufactured and shipped to the region, though he did not provide evidence or specify which munitions he was referring to.
His comments followed reports that he confronted defence secretary Pete Hegseth during a Cabinet meeting at Camp David last week over alleged shortages of critical weapons.
According to the Washington Post, citing two unnamed sources familiar with the discussion, Trump told Hegseth he felt misled because he believed the issue "had been fixed".
The newspaper reported that Hegseth defended his handling of the matter and sought to place responsibility on his deputy, Stephen Feinberg.
Trump later lashed out at the reports, accusing the media of publishing "treasonous statements"."The 'leakers' of these treasonous statements are being hunted down," he wrote. "Long term jail sentences will be sought!"
new_text:
A furious Donald Trump has hit out at "leakers" as he condemned "treasonous" reports that the US has almost depleted its stock of precision long-range missiles in its war with Iran.
The president claimed the US still has "massive amounts" of the expensive munitions, adding that "large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the US as needed".
"The 'leakers' of these treasonous statements are being hunted down. Long term jail sentences will be sought!" he added in the Truth Social tirade.
Trump also denied US media reports that he had reprimanded defence secretary Pete Hegseth during a Cabinet meeting in which low ammunition stockpiles were discussed.
Two sources told Reuters news agency that the military's surface-to-surface weapons, known as Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM) had been "virtually all" used in its war against Tehran.
Meanwhile, the US president claimed the Strait of Hormuz is "sort of open" and predicted that the war with Iran will "end pretty soon" as negotiations continue between Tehran and Oman.
The US president said although the shipping route was under US control, there was a possibility that Tehran could still "shoot things" or "drop a mine."
Iran feels time is on its side as negotiations with US continue
To borrow a phrase from Donald Trump's own theory of geopolitics, Iran believes it holds the cards.
"They started the war, but its end was never with them. We always decide for ourselves when it ends," Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's chief negotiator, posted on social media. "Iran is going after the enemy's defeat - not an agreement."
He said a surprise Iranian attack on Jordan in July "compensated" for a drop in oil prices. That contributed to the collapse of an interim agreement reached in June that had offered significant concessions to Iran, including a US waiver to sell oil internationally and the promise of broader sanctions relief.
Iran has repeatedly said the Strait of Hormuz will not go back to being an open waterway, and that it will keep attacking ships trying to transit without its permission. Iran's joint military command has called it an "unbreakable red line."
"For Iran, the Strait of Hormuz has become a strategic lever for deterrence, maintaining the regional balance of power, and reshaping the security rules in the Persian Gulf," said Mostafa Najafi, a Tehran-based security analyst.
That poses a major obstacle to ending the war, much less resolving the even more complex, long-standing dispute over Iran's nuclear program.
"The atomic issue, because of the conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, has been pushed to the side, and in reality, that is in Iran's interests," said Rahman Ghahremanpour, an Iran-based analyst. Control of the strait would give Iran leverage if the nuclear talks resume, he added.
Abu Dhabi oil company says it is impacted by unprovoked attacks
An oil company in Abu Dhabi has hit out at what it called unprovoked attacks on its vessels.
The Abu Dhabi National Oil Company said on Friday it continued to be significantly impacted by the attacks, but was taking measures to protect its people, assets and operations while meeting customer requirements as much as possible.
ADNOC said in a statement that 15 of its vessels had been attacked by missiles and drones while transiting the Strait of Hormuz since the start of the conflict, including three this week, leaving one crew member dead and 20 injured.
Trump hosts mining CEOs amid worries over depleting weapons stockpiles
US president Donald Trump yesterday convened executives from leading mining companies at the State Department to strengthen domestic and allied supplies of critical minerals, a key component of the nation's security and industrial strategy.
The administration seeks to replenish weapons stockpiles, depleted during the Iran conflict, and reduce US dependence on Chinese supply chains for essential minerals like rare earths, tungsten, and germanium, which are vital for advanced military systems.
The White House needs critical minerals to replenish weapons stockpiles depleted during the Iran conflict and reduce US dependence on Chinese supply chains.
The gathering included approximately 200 participants, featuring executives from companies such as Resolution Copper, MP Materials, and Century Aluminum, alongside high-ranking officials including Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Several executives came with gifts for Trump. Tom Albanese, chairman of deep-sea mining firm American Ocean Minerals, gave Trump a gold replica of a nodule that the company hopes to mine from the Pacific seabed. Trump last year said he may bypass the UN-backed International Seabed Authority and issue international seabed mining licenses.
Jim Litinsky, CEO of rare earths firm MP Materials, which is financially supported by the Pentagon, gave Trump magnets that had been produced for General Motors in the company's Texas plant.
How does Oman-Iran deal give Tehran an upper hand
Iran says it is close to reaching a deal with Oman to manage the Strait of Hormuz, which runs between the two countries.
But it would be conditional on the US lifting its blockade on the crucial waterway.
It would formalise its control over what had been an open international waterway before the war, one that carried a fifth of the world's traded oil and gas.
Abdolreza Davari, an analyst who once advised former president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, said Iran's effective control of the strait has given it leverage with the US and regional countries that can help guarantee its security.
"More than revenue from the strait, Iran wants to confirm its management and sovereignty over the strait," he said by phone from Tehran.
Formal control over even part of the strait would be a clear win for Iran and a loss for the US, which has yet to accomplish some of its various and shifting goals in the war.
It would also deal a blow to global norms on freedom of navigation and set a precedent that much of the world would find disturbing - that nations can shut down trade choke points at will.
China, which buys oil from Iran and has influence over it, said as recently as May that "normal and safe passage" through the strait should be restored.
Houthis strike Marib again as UN warns Yemen nearing wider conflict
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis launched ballistic missiles and drones at displacement camps and residential neighbourhoods in the city of Marib on Friday, killing two people and wounding 14 others, state news agency SABA reported, citing local authorities.
The Houthis said they had targeted Saudi-backed forces, depots, vehicles and military equipment at the Sahn al-Jinn camp in the city with missiles and drones.
The attacks came a day after at least 30 Yemeni government troops were killed in strikes on military camps in Marib and Hadramawt provinces, according to government sources, in one of the deadliest escalations in months.
The Houthis also claimed responsibility for Thursday's attacks, saying they struck Saudi military deployments in the two provinces after detecting what they described as a large Saudi military buildup ahead of an escalation against areas under their control.
US special envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg said on Friday that the latest attacks in Marib and Hadramawt, together with renewed attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, had left Yemen at its greatest risk of renewed large-scale conflict since the UN-brokered truce in April 2022.

Trump's Chairman of the Joint Chiefs seeking 'off-ramp' from Iran war, report says
President Donald Trump's Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, General Dan Caine, is seeking an "off-ramp " from the ongoing war in Iran, according to a new report.
Caine has privately told other top administration officials that the country needs to find a way to exit the war, according to CNN, which cited three sources familiar with the matter.
Despite Trump claiming throughout the war that a peace deal, which would include his demand that Iran never obtain a nuclear weapon, was within reach, fighting has continued for more than five months.
"Caine is looking for an off ramp," one of CNN's sources said.
The general's meetings with Trump officials, including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, are just to make clear the limitations and pitfalls of different military options, according to the sources.
Putin discusses Gulf situation with UAE president
Russian president Vladimir Putin has spoken to United Arab Emirates president Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the Kremlin said on Friday.
The pair discussed the situation in the Gulf, where Iranian and Omani negotiators are seeking to fix an impasse over the Strait of Hormuz.
They also discussed the war on Ukraine, with Putin expressing his gratitude to the United Arab Emirates for its role in organising exchanges of prisoners of war and detainees between Russia and Ukraine, the Kremlin said.
Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia sign a mutual defence agreement
Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia have signed a mutual defense agreement, at a time the Iran-backed Houthi rebels have stepped up attacks on Saudi-linked targets.
Oil-rich Saudi Arabia, nuclear power Pakistan and Turkey, which has Nato's second-largest army and a rapidly growing defence industry, signed a mutual defense agreement on Friday.
The deal stipulates that an armed attack on either of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against them all.
It was signed during a meeting in Saudi Arabia between Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistan's prime minister Shehbaz Sharif, Pakistan's foreign ministry said.
"The Agreement is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression," the ministry said in a statement.
The deal comes at a time when Saudi Arabia, whose critical infrastructure and oil facilities have come under attack as part of the war in Iran, has been looking to diversify its defense partnerships.
